name: BEND
description: Benchmark of DNA language models on biologically meaningful genome annotation tasks -- chromatin accessibility, histone modification, CpG methylation and variant effects -- rather than on synthetic proxies.
notes: Finding worth carrying: DNA LM embeddings approach expert methods on some tasks but capture limited long-range information. `year: 2023` is the arXiv posting; the venue is ICLR 2024. No DOI -- ICLR mints none, so `paper_id` falls back to the arXiv ID per schema §2.2.

name: DART-Eval
description: Regulatory-DNA focused evaluation suite comparing DNA language models against ab initio sequence baselines across zero-shot, probed and fine-tuned regimes.
notes: The finding that makes this the most useful benchmark in the seed: annotation-agnostic DNA LMs are inconsistent and show no compelling gain over ab initio baselines. Because it includes those baselines, it functions as a critique of the DNA LM programme as much as a benchmark of it. Its author list overlaps with ChromBPNet's through Kundaje, which is why model:chrombpnet derives as partially-independent rather than externally benchmarked.

name: GENEB
description: Unified probing benchmark covering 40 genomic foundation models across 100 tasks in 13 functional categories, with leaderboard artifacts built by CI from reviewed submissions rather than hand-edited.
notes: The headline finding is the reason CFCR does not store scores: aggregate leaderboards are unstable, rankings vary sharply across task categories, and scale gives modest and inconsistent gains. Any single number CFCR copied here would be misleading within a release cycle. Submission-open and CI-built, so it stays current in a way a curated table cannot.

name: JASPAR 2024
description: Open-access database of curated, non-redundant transcription factor binding profiles stored as position frequency matrices, with taxonomic coverage across six groups and an API and bulk downloads.
notes: `year: 2023` is the Nucleic Acids Research issue year for the release branded "JASPAR 2024" -- the release name and the publication year disagree, which is normal for the NAR database issue and a recurring trap when citing these. The name is kept as the community uses it.

name: Borzoi training intervals
description: The genomic intervals and train/validation/test fold assignments used to train Borzoi, released as TSV for human and mouse.
notes: Catalogued separately from model:borzoi because fold assignment is what makes an independent evaluation comparable. Anyone benchmarking against Borzoi who re-splits the genome themselves is not measuring the same thing. Record counts are deliberately null: the source release reports 55,497 human and 49,369 mouse intervals, which is two numbers and one `n_records` column, and neither figure was confirmable from the repository metadata.

name: Enformer training intervals
description: The genomic intervals and fold assignments used to train Enformer, released as TSV for human and mouse.
notes: Same reasoning as dataset:borzoi-data. Useful mainly for like-for-like comparison against the Enformer line; the source release reports 38,171 human and 33,521 mouse intervals, again unconfirmed from repository metadata.

name: Replogle 2022 genome-scale Perturb-seq atlas
description: Genome-scale Perturb-seq screens in human cell lines, knocking down essentially all expressed genes and reading out single-cell transcriptomes, providing the reference training and evaluation data for perturbation response models.
notes: Catalogued on the `what` axis as the dataset that most perturbation models in the adjacent literature are trained or evaluated on, including model:gears. CFCR holds the pointer; the Stegle catalogue holds the method landscape.

name: AlphaGenome
description: Unified DNA sequence model taking 1 Mb of input and predicting thousands of functional genomic tracks at base resolution across multiple modalities, covering regulatory variant effect prediction in one model rather than a per-assay family.
notes: The only api-only entry in the seed, and the reason that tier exists: there are no weights to download and no license to read, so reproducibility and long-term availability rest on Google continuing to serve the endpoint. Independently evaluated for fine-mapping reproducibility by Sweeney & Kang alongside Borzoi, Enformer and Sei.

name: Borzoi
description: Predicts cell-type- and tissue-specific RNA-seq coverage from DNA sequence over a 524 kb context, scoring variant effects across transcription, splicing and polyadenylation from the one model. Successor to Enformer with finer output resolution and RNA-seq heads.
notes: `year: 2023` is the first public release (bioRxiv); the Nature Genetics paper carries a 2025 issue year. Trained with the Baskerville framework rather than the Enformer codebase, so the two are not drop-in comparable despite the lineage.

name: ChromBPNet
description: Base-resolution model of chromatin accessibility profiles that factorizes out assay-specific enzyme bias, letting learned cis-regulatory sequence syntax and TF motif contributions be read off the prediction directly.
notes: Narrow input window compared with the Enformer/Borzoi line -- it models local accessibility syntax rather than long-range regulation, which is why it answers a different `where` question despite sharing the axis. Evaluated as an ab initio baseline in DART-Eval, whose author list overlaps with this one through Kundaje, so the derivation should land it at `partially-independent` rather than `externally-benchmarked`.

name: Enformer
description: Predicts gene expression and chromatin tracks from DNA sequence by combining dilated convolutions with transformer blocks, integrating regulatory information from up to 100 kb away. Established the long-context interval model as the dominant architecture for sequence-to-function prediction.
notes: The reference point the whole interval-model literature argues with. Two independent Nature Genetics analyses (Tang/Toneyan/Koo and Huang et al.) found it explains personal transcriptome variation poorly despite strong cross-locus accuracy -- the across-individual vs across-gene distinction is the single most important caveat to communicate to anyone picking it up. Replicate checkpoints and the many community ports are deliberately not separate entities; see model:flashzoi for one that is.

name: Evo 2
description: Genome language model trained on 3 trillion DNA base pairs spanning all domains of life, with 7B and 40B parameter variants, a 1 million token context window at single-nucleotide resolution, and both variant-effect scoring and genome design applications.
notes: Trained across all domains of life rather than one clade, so `organism` carries the local term `multi-species` -- no single NCBITaxon node says this without claiming a specific clade. Two parameter variants ship together as one release, carried as the 7B-40B range rather than collapsed to a single figure.

name: Flashzoi
description: Re-implementation of Borzoi substituting rotary positional encodings and FlashAttention-2 for relative positional encodings, giving over 3-fold faster training and inference and up to 2.4-fold lower memory use while maintaining or improving accuracy.
notes: A port under its own name, so a separate entity with `variant_of` rather than a Borzoi link -- the granularity rule's worked case. Weights for all four Flashzoi and Borzoi replicates are published together under MIT; the replicates are one entity, not four. Licensed more permissively than Borzoi itself, which matters for downstream reuse.

name: GEARS
description: Graph neural network predicting transcriptional outcomes of multigene perturbations, including combinations never seen in training, by combining a gene co-expression graph with a knowledge graph of gene ontology relations.
notes: Deliberately shallow. Perturbation modelling is covered properly by the Stegle group's living catalogue (>152 methods, Nat Rev Genet 2026) and CFCR points outward rather than competing -- see the `website` link. GEARS is here as the representative entry so the `what` axis is not empty, not as the start of a perturbation index. `architecture` required a new vocabulary term: GNN is absent from the schema §3.1 enum, and it is the dominant architecture on this axis.

name: Nucleotide Transformer
description: Family of transformer DNA language models pretrained on human and multi-species genomes, released as a set of checkpoints from 50M to 2.5B parameters and evaluated by probing on downstream regulatory tasks.
notes: The `open-weights` case, and the reason that tier is distinct from `open-source`: inference code is on GitHub, but the published checkpoints carry CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0, which forbids commercial use and imposes share-alike on derivatives. Anyone building a product on this needs to read the license before the paper. Checkpoint sizes span two orders of magnitude, which is what `n_parameters_min`/`_max` exist to carry: the entity is the family, not one checkpoint, so filtering on size means filtering on the range.

name: DelRosso 2023 human transcriptional effector domains
description: Large-scale mapping and systematic mutagenesis of human transcriptional effector domains by HT-recruit, establishing sequence determinants of activation and repression across a broad survey of annotated domains.
notes: The mutagenesis arm is what distinguishes this from a pure discovery screen: it reports which residues matter, not only which domains work, which is the difference between a parts list and a design rule. `n_records` is null -- the domain count is reported across several screen arms in the paper and was not confirmable from open metadata.

name: EpiFactors 2022 epigenetic regulators
description: Curated database of human epigenetic regulators, protein complexes and their functional annotation, covering chromatin-modifying enzymes, remodelers and reader domains.
notes: Curated annotation rather than a screen, so `dominant_validation_level` is `predicted` -- the entries are literature-asserted functional assignments, not measurements in a recruitment assay. That difference is exactly what the validation-level vocabulary exists to carry, and it matters when picking a chromatin remodeler to build an eCR from.

name: Tycko 2025 compact effector domains
description: HT-recruit screen of compact activation and repression domains measured across multiple cellular contexts; 38 CD2 activation domains and 1,223 CD43 repression domains.
notes: `year: 2024` is the verified Nature Biotechnology issue year. The collection is known in the lab as "Tycko 2025" and `ecr_lib_source_key: Tycko_2025` is kept unchanged because it is the join key into eCR_mod_lib's `source_screen` column -- changing it would break the deep link for cosmetic consistency.

name: CUT&RUN targeted in situ genome-wide profiling
description: The reference CUT&RUN protocol for targeted in situ chromatin profiling at high efficiency from low cell numbers, hosted on protocols.io by the originating lab.
notes: The `external` origin case, and the model for how protocols should be catalogued: a real protocols.io DOI, maintained by the authors, versioned upstream. CFCR adds discovery and trust metadata, nothing else.

name: Low-input CUT&RUN for sorted MEF populations
description: CUT&RUN adapted for 5,000-20,000 sorted cells, optimized for histone marks during MEF reprogramming timecourses.
notes: The `cfc-lab` origin case. `protocol_doi` is null: schema §9 shows 10.17504/protocols.io.xxxxx, which is a placeholder, and no real DOI has been minted yet. This entity is therefore the one seed record that will fail the "every entity has a primary paper" QC check -- it is the whitelisted exception the check needs to support, since an unpublished in-house protocol has no paper by definition.
